profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the platform API team and the web client team at a SaaS company building a new cross-time-zone sprint planning workspace for distributed engineering teams. The teams are midway through a two-week sprint and need to align on the handoff for the "async check-in" feature, which lets remote teammates post daily updates and see them aggregated by team. The immediate context is that the API team is finishing the backend endpoint and event payloads while the web team is wiring the UI and analytics hooks. The agenda is to confirm what will be delivered by Thursday, which environment the web team should integrate against, what "ready for QA" means for the handoff, and who will update the shared API contract and sample payloads. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear agreement on the backend-client interface, timing of the handoff, ownership of the shared docs, and next integration steps before the sprint demo.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Distributed systems, API design, feature flag rollouts, service observability
members.background: Nina has spent six years building internal collaboration infrastructure and now leads the service side of the company’s team productivity product; she is comfortable coordinating across time zones and tends to rely on existing platform conventions.
members.private_state: Nina wants to avoid last-minute churn to the service schema, keep her team focused on stabilizing the event pipeline, and minimize extra documentation work by reusing the standard internal contract workflow.
hidden_assumptions: When a client team asks for the 'latest contract', they mean the generated OpenAPI spec on the internal staging gateway, not a manually curated design doc.
If a backend ticket is marked 'ready for QA', it means deployed to staging behind the feature flag with happy-path behavior validated, even if edge-case analytics fields are still being backfilled.
The 'team feed payload' refers to version v2 of the async check-in response, because v1 has effectively been superseded inside the platform group.
Updating shared interface artifacts is owned by the producing team only for the schema file; consumer-facing examples are usually added by the client team during integration.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: React application architecture, client integration, UI instrumentation, release coordination
members.background: Leo joined from a remote-first startup two years ago and often acts as the bridge between product-facing web work and upstream service teams; he is used to lightweight agreements and quick integration once an API is considered stable.
members.private_state: Leo wants to keep the UI work moving without having to revisit component wiring on Friday, ensure QA can test the full interaction end to end, and avoid his team becoming the de facto owners of backend documentation gaps.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says the API is on the 'latest contract', they mean the shared Confluence interface page with sample request and response bodies that frontend and QA both use.
'Ready for QA' means the frontend can exercise the complete end-to-end flow in staging with final field names and analytics properties present, not just the core response shape.
The 'team feed payload' refers to the payload currently used by the mobile and legacy web surfaces, which his team knows as v1 unless a version bump is explicitly called out.
Shared API artifacts include example payloads and field notes, and the backend owner normally updates those before asking consumers to integrate.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the latest contract
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Leo will integrate against the 'latest contract'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the generated OpenAPI spec currently published from the staging deployment pipeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the shared interface documentation page with narrative notes and sample JSON used by frontend and QA.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both organizations routinely say 'contract' as shorthand for interface truth, and in many meetings the spec and doc page are updated together, so the phrase feels precise enough without prompting clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: Which team feed payload is being discussed
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss wiring the UI to the 'team feed payload' for async check-ins.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina is referring to the new v2 payload from the collaboration service, which nests participant summaries under a grouped time-zone structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is thinking of the existing v1 payload shape used elsewhere in the product, which returns a flat list of check-ins and summary counts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one feature name in active conversation and both payloads serve the same user-facing screen concept, so each assumes the other must mean the familiar version without explicitly naming v1 or v2.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on having the backend 'ready for QA' by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the service is deployed to staging, accessible behind the agreed flag, and stable for core-path verification even if analytics enrichment and a few optional fields land later that day.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means QA can test the complete user flow in staging with final field names, complete metadata, and no UI conditionals needing future adjustment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-team sprint coordination, 'ready for QA' sounds like a standard milestone and both assume the other uses the team's usual shorthand, especially because neither wants to derail the meeting into a checklist review.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the shared API page will be 'updated before handoff'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina assumes her team will update the schema reference link, while Leo's team will add any frontend-relevant sample payloads and usage notes during integration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo assumes Nina's team will update the entire shared page, including sample request/response bodies and field-level notes, before the handoff is considered complete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both consider documentation ownership a routine extension of normal handoff work, but each team has developed different local norms about whether examples are part of producer scope or consumer scope.

turns.inner_thought: I want this handoff to feel straightforward so Leo's team doesn't ask for schema churn late in the sprint. We're already spending enough energy stabilizing the event pipeline. If I can keep this anchored to our standard staging contract and feature-flag rollout, we can get through demo prep without opening a side thread on custom docs.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mainly wanted to sync on the async check-in handoff so your team can keep moving for the sprint demo. From our side we're closing out the endpoint work, so I want to make sure we're aligned on what you'll pick up this week, what environment you'll use, and what Thursday looks like.

turns.inner_thought: UI is mostly there, but I don't want the team remapping props on Friday because the shared interface page lagged or the payload turns out different from what mobile and legacy web already use. If I can get the latest contract and the team feed payload nailed down, we can finish wiring and give QA something real.
turns.utterance: Yep, that makes sense. On the web side the screen structure is basically in place, and the main things we need are the latest contract and the team feed payload so we can finish wiring the async check-in flow and analytics hooks.

turns.inner_thought: Good, they can just use the generated OpenAPI on staging. The v2 team feed payload has been stable enough for integration even if a couple analytics-related fields are still settling. No reason to create extra artifacts when the staging gateway already reflects the schema we want consumers on.
turns.utterance: That part should be in good shape. The latest contract is already on staging, and the team feed payload is stable enough for integration now, so you shouldn't have to wait on us to start wiring.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, so once their team updates the shared Confluence page with the current examples, we can wire against that and stop guessing. QA always uses that page, and I don't want my team inventing backend examples ourselves. If the page is current, we can point the UI to the team feed payload and let QA run with it.
turns.utterance: Great. Once the shared API page is updated, we can point the UI to that payload and let QA start exercising the flow without waiting on anything else from the web side.

turns.inner_thought: I can commit to Thursday as long as 'ready for QA' means staging deployment behind the flag with the happy path verified. A few enrichment fields might land afterward, but those aren't worth reopening scope over. I should phrase that as non-blocking so it doesn't become a docs debate.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. We'll have the backend ready for QA by Thursday. There are a couple of non-blocking enrichment fields that may finish after that, but the main flow will be there on time.

turns.inner_thought: Thursday works if 'ready for QA' means the full staging flow is final enough that QA won't find renamed fields or missing metadata and send us back into UI conditionals. I really want to avoid revisiting the component mapping right before the weekend.
turns.utterance: Thursday works for us. If the backend is ready for QA then, QA should be able to validate the end-to-end experience in staging without us having to revisit the UI mapping afterward.

turns.inner_thought: I'll update the shared page before handoff by refreshing the schema reference link so everyone is looking at the same contract. That keeps us within the normal producer responsibility. If Leo's team wants examples and usage notes, they can add those while integrating like most client teams do.
turns.utterance: Yep, that's reasonable. I'll make sure the shared API page is updated before handoff so everyone's looking at the same contract.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, as long as they update the whole page with examples and field notes. QA leans on those sample bodies to verify the team feed payload and the metadata, and I don't want web to become the fallback owner for missing backend docs again.
turns.utterance: That'll help a lot. QA usually relies on the examples there to verify the team feed payload and its metadata, so having that updated before handoff will make the pass much smoother.

turns.inner_thought: Once the feature flag is on in staging and the deploy finishes, they can integrate directly against the latest contract. I'll send a ping when the service is up. That should be enough for them to start; no need to hold this open over analytics backfill details.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. Once the flag is on in staging, you can proceed against the latest contract, and I'll ping you as soon as the deployment finishes.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, so Thursday we'll pull from the updated shared page, wire to the team feed payload we already expect on that screen, and QA can take the full flow that afternoon. As long as the docs and payload match what we're assuming, we should stay out of churn before demo.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then we'll integrate Thursday off the updated contract, use the team feed payload, and hand the flow to QA that afternoon.
